profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at an academic medical center reviewing a near-final protocol for a multiclinic primary-care study on research participation effects in antibiotic prescribing for acute sinusitis. The draft draws on the Hawthorne-effect review to justify a three-condition design: routine EHR extraction only, clinician questionnaire plus EHR extraction, and observed clinic sessions plus EHR extraction. The meeting is not meant to re-debate the overall scientific premise; instead, the agenda is to check whether the current design package is solid enough for internal methods committee submission, with attention to comparator periods, whether the design still reflects routine care, whether the analysis plan is sufficiently complete, and whether the observation procedures are acceptably low-burden. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to submit this month and a concise list of revisions to make before circulation.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Primary-care antibiotic stewardship trials, pragmatic study design, clinical implementation research
members.background: Maya leads outpatient stewardship projects across three affiliated family-medicine clinics and has previously run low-burden EHR-based quality-improvement studies that were later adapted into research protocols.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol to stay clinic-feasible and close to normal workflow so site leaders will cooperate, and she is quietly trying to avoid revisions that would push launch past the next respiratory season.
hidden_assumptions: If clinician behavior is measured during standard clinic operations without adding extra clinical steps, the study is still observing routine behavior even if clinicians have already signed consent and know data collection is underway.
The baseline period is the 12-week retrospective EHR window from the prior winter before any clinician-facing study contact.

An analysis plan is complete once the main comparisons, covariates, and modeling approach are named in the protocol; table shells and edge-case handling can wait for the manual of procedures or SAP addendum.
Non-disruptive observation means the research assistant enters the exam room but remains silent and physically unobtrusive so visit flow is not materially altered.

members.name: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
members.role: Behavioral Epidemiologist and Methods Committee Reviewer
members.expertise: Measurement reactivity, survey effects, observer effects, bias in quasi-experimental and embedded clinical studies
members.background: Samuel specializes in behavior change induced by study procedures and has consulted on several NIH-funded trials involving clinician observation, patient-reported measures, and protocol-induced artifacts.
members.private_state: He wants the protocol to survive committee scrutiny as interpretable rather than merely feasible, and he is concerned that loosely specified operational details will make any estimated participation effect impossible to read.
hidden_assumptions: Routine behavior means behavior recorded before clinicians are brought into a formal research context, especially before consent and study briefing create anticipatory reactivity.
The baseline period should be a prospective run-in during the same respiratory season after clinics are enrolled but before questionnaire or observation exposure begins.
An analysis plan is not complete unless reviewers can see the exact reporting structure, including dummy tables, missing-data handling, outlier rules, and how repeated visits will be counted.

Non-disruptive observation means observation occurs from outside the exam room whenever possible, such as from the nurses' station or through workflow tracing, so the patient-clinician interaction itself is not physically altered by an additional person.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the design should preserve or capture 'routine behavior.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means visits conducted during normal clinic hours with ordinary staffing and no added clinical tasks, even if clinicians have already consented and know the study is active.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means behavior observed before formal study enrollment cues themselves can alter conduct, so once clinicians have consented or been briefed, the behavior is no longer fully routine.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like standard pragmatic-trial language, and both are sincerely trying to avoid artificial workflow changes; because neither is disputing the overall low-burden design, the deeper difference about whether research awareness itself breaks routineness remains hidden.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the baseline period' when discussing the comparator data.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the already-available retrospective 12-week EHR window from the previous winter before any study contact.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to a prospective pre-exposure run-in at the start of the study season after site activation but before questionnaires or observation begin.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Baseline is a routine term in clinical research and both candidate periods plausibly function as pre-exposure comparators, so the phrase feels precise enough even though the time windows imply very different sources of reactivity and seasonal comparability.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the analysis plan to be complete
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether 'the analysis plan is complete' for methods committee review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the protocol already specifies the core contrasts between study conditions, the regression framework, and the main adjustment variables, which is enough for committee review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means completeness requires reviewer-visible reporting details such as table shells, missing-data rules, repeat-visit counting conventions, and handling of clinicians with partial observation exposure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to treating 'analysis plan' as a single deliverable, and each believes their own threshold is the ordinary one for internal review; because they are talking about completeness rather than content disagreements, the mismatch sounds like agreement.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the observation approach should be 'non-disruptive.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means a silent research assistant can sit in the exam room corner during selected sinusitis visits as long as no questions are asked and throughput is preserved.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the observer should stay outside the room and document workflow exposure indirectly whenever feasible, because simply adding a person inside the room changes the encounter environment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Non-disruptive is a reassuring, familiar phrase in clinical operations, and both imagine a low-profile observer; since the meeting focuses on whether observation is acceptably low-burden rather than on room placement as a primary design decision, each defaults to a different 'obvious' implementation.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to land as a practical, nearly finished package. The whole point is to compare EHR-only, questionnaire, and observation conditions without adding clinic tasks or slowing visits, and to me that still preserves routine behavior even after clinicians have consented, as long as care delivery itself is unchanged. If Samuel sees this as submission-ready with only light edits, we can keep the launch on track for the next respiratory season.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The draft is designed to preserve routine behavior while comparing the EHR-only, questionnaire, and observation conditions, and what I want to sort out today is whether the package is ready to go to methods committee this month.

turns.inner_thought: The concept is solid, but the committee will care most about whether the participation effects can actually be interpreted. For me that hinges on the baseline period being a true pre-exposure comparator in the current study sequence, and on the analysis plan being complete in the reviewer-facing sense, not just naming models. I should keep this framed as making the submission durable rather than reopening the design.
turns.utterance: I think the overall design is strong. My sense is that the committee will mainly want reassurance that the comparator periods are framed cleanly and that the supporting materials are developed enough for them to read the participation effects clearly.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he's talking about framing rather than redesign. The baseline period is already sitting there in the prior winter EHR data, which is exactly why this stays low-burden and fast. And because it predates any clinician-facing study contact, that comparator captures routine behavior in the cleanest way without adding a run-in phase that would burn time and goodwill.
turns.utterance: That helps. One reason I feel fairly comfortable is that the baseline period is straightforward to work with, which lets us keep the site asks light and stay aligned with the goal of capturing routine behavior.

turns.inner_thought: She seems comfortable with the same basic idea: baseline should function as the clean before state. I still want the protocol to say plainly that the baseline period is the pre-exposure comparator before the more reactive pieces come in, otherwise reviewers may not know where to anchor interpretation.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think the key will be to describe the baseline period in a way that clearly signals its role as the pre-exposure comparator, because that's usually where reviewers orient themselves.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine; wording I can do. I just don't want language that implies everything after study start stops being routine. From the clinic perspective, if staffing, scheduling, and care processes remain ordinary and there are no extra clinical steps, we're still seeing routine behavior. That's the pragmatic frame the site leaders will accept.
turns.utterance: Right. And from the implementation side, I do think we can still say the design stays close to routine behavior, since the clinics aren't being asked to change how visits are run.

turns.inner_thought: Operationally, sure, it's pragmatic. But I need the write-up to mark the line between routine behavior and study exposure, because once clinicians have entered a formal research context I don't consider that fully routine anymore. Better to ask for cleaner language than to argue definitions outright.
turns.utterance: That seems reasonable. I think the write-up just needs to be careful about how it uses the routine behavior language across the different parts of the design so readers can follow the sequence without overinterpreting it.

turns.inner_thought: So far this still sounds manageable. On methods, I want to hold the line that the analysis plan is complete enough for committee review because the core comparisons, covariates, and mixed-effects approach are already in the protocol. If we turn this into a demand for a full SAP now, we'll lose the month.
turns.utterance: On the methods section, my read is that the analysis plan is basically complete already. The protocol identifies the main comparisons, the adjustment strategy, and the modeling framework, which is usually the level this committee needs.

turns.inner_thought: Not quite, by my standards. The analysis plan isn't really complete until reviewers can see the reporting structure and operational rules, otherwise they'll worry that key choices are floating. But I can phrase this as a modest strengthening request instead of saying it's incomplete.
turns.utterance: I agree the backbone is there. I think it will read as more complete to the committee if the next version makes the reporting structure a little more visible, even briefly.

turns.inner_thought: A brief add-on I can live with. Let me shift to the observation arm, because the clinics already accepted what I have in mind: an RA in the exam room, silent and out of the way, during selected sinusitis visits. As long as patient flow isn't affected, I consider that non-disruptive observation and still feasible for launch.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. The other area I wanted to check is the observation arm, since the clinics have said they're comfortable with a non-disruptive observation approach during selected sessions as long as flow stays intact.

turns.inner_thought: Non-disruptive observation is exactly the right phrase, but I need it to mean that the encounter itself isn't physically altered more than necessary—ideally observed from outside the room or through indirect workflow capture when possible. I'll keep it at the principle level so it sounds like wording, not redesign.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. I would just make sure the description of the non-disruptive observation approach emphasizes that the encounter itself remains as untouched as possible.

turns.inner_thought: Good—he's still talking about description, not structural changes. I can add a short clarification paragraph on the baseline period and routine behavior language, plus a compact appendix so the analysis plan looks polished enough. Keep the revisions narrow, circulate this week, and don't trigger anything that delays launch.
turns.utterance: In that case, my preference would be to do one focused revision pass and still submit this month—tighten a bit of the framing, add a short methods attachment, and make sure the design narrative reads cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: That's probably the right compromise. If those edits really clarify the comparator framing, make the analysis plan feel complete, and describe the observation piece in a way the committee reads as non-disruptive, the package should survive review even if I still want more detail later.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that's a reasonable path. With that kind of revision, the submission should be in good enough shape for committee review and a lot less likely to generate avoidable questions.
